The bell over the door hadn't worked in three weeks. Jay kept meaning to fix it, but the silence had become useful—he could tell a future tourist from a local by whether they paused at the threshold or walked straight to the counter.

Morning light came through the front window at a shallow angle. Jay wiped down the display case nearest the door, adjusting mid-grade clef on black velvet. The pieces shifted under light—crystalline, refractive, a quality buyers called resonance. He didn't pretend to understand. He just knew what sold.

The shop was narrow, twelve feet across, wedged between a nail salon and a bodega. His uncle had run it for thirty years before leaving it to Jay—the space, the inventory, debts that took two years to clear. The debts were gone now. The inventory was mostly replaced. Only the photographs on the walls remained: buildings tilted, streets cracked, a bridge collapsed into the bay. The [[1989 earthquake]], old disaster made safe by distance. Tourists loved them. They'd stand photographing the photographs, trying to capture some quality Jay couldn't name.

Telegraph was quiet at this hour. A woman pushed a cart loaded with flattened cardboard. A delivery truck idled outside the taqueria. The future traffic wouldn't arrive until noon—groups of three or four drifting through, buying clef and vintage electronics, photographing storefronts. They tipped well. They rarely made eye contact.

The door opened. No pause at the threshold, no uncertain scan of the interior. Just a woman walking toward the counter like she knew exactly where she was going.

She was younger than most of the future visitors—late twenties, maybe, though that didn't mean much. Good bone structure, sharp eyes, hair cropped close to her skull. She wore clothes that almost passed for local: denim jacket, boots, a shirt that looked ordinary until you noticed how the fabric caught light. Everything a half-beat off, like a costume assembled from excellent research.

"I want to see the high-grade," she said. No greeting. Her accent was hard to place—vowels flattened, consonants precise.

Jay pulled the tray from beneath the register. Six pieces on gray silk, each one dense with that interior light buyers paid for. She leaned over the case, studying them without touching. Most tourists grabbed immediately, held pieces up to their faces, asked questions they didn't want answered. This one just looked.

"That one," she said, pointing to a pale amber piece near the edge. Not the most expensive, but close. "How much?"

"Twelve hundred."

She nodded like the number meant nothing. Reached into her jacket pocket and pulled out—

A phone. Old model, cracked screen, the kind you could buy for forty dollars at the [[Fruitvale flea market]]. She stared at it, turned it over in her hands. Tapped the dark screen. Nothing happened.

"It needs to—" Jay started.

"I know what it needs." Her voice went flat. She pressed the side button, held it too long. The screen flickered, died. She tried again, jabbing at it now, and Jay watched her face change—confusion first, then something harder. Embarrassment sharpening into anger.

"The passcode," Jay said. "You have to—"

"I have the passcode." She wasn't looking at him now. Her thumb moved across the cracked glass in small circles, a gesture that meant nothing to the device. Like she was trying to wake something that should respond to touch alone.

The morning light shifted. Outside, a bus groaned past on Telegraph. Jay watched her hands—the way they moved with confidence that kept failing, muscle memory for something that wasn't there.

"Look," he said. "The screen. You swipe up first, then enter the numbers."

She went still. When she looked up, her expression had closed off entirely. "I know how it works."

"Okay."

"I've used one before."

"Sure."

She set the phone on the counter between them. Her jaw was tight now, and Jay recognized something in her face—the particular shame of being caught out, of needing help you can't admit you need. He'd seen it before, in tourists who couldn't read a paper menu or work a doorknob or understand why a card wouldn't scan without a signature.

"Take it," he said.

She blinked. "What?"

"The clef." He slid the amber piece across the glass toward her. "Take it. We'll figure out the payment later."

"I can pay."

"I know you can." He met her eyes. "But not with that phone. And not right now. So take it, come back when you've sorted things out, and we'll settle up then."

She studied him the way she'd studied the clef—looking for the trick, the angle. Finding neither.

"I'm Tan," she said finally.

"Jay." He didn't offer his hand—learned early that the gesture confused more than half of them.

She held the amber piece up to the window. The refraction caught her face, pale lines moving across her cheekbones like something alive. Most tourists would have pocketed it by now, moved toward the door, forgotten his name before reaching the sidewalk. She was still here.

"The phone's not mine," she said. "Someone told me I'd need one. For payments." She pushed it across the counter like it had burned her. "I'm not used to them."

"Neural interface?"

Her eyes sharpened. "You know about—"

"I sell to future traffic all day. I know what you're used to." He picked up his rag, worked at a fingerprint near the register. "Phones are harder for you. Too many steps, too slow. Like asking someone to write letters when they're used to—"

"Worse," she said. "Like learning to walk again with different legs."

Outside, a man was setting up a folding table on the corner—[[bootleg temporal maps]], hand-drawn, wildly inaccurate, sold to tourists who didn't know better. Jay watched Tan track the movement through the window, her attention catching on details he'd stopped seeing years ago.

"Why would you trust me to come back?" she asked.

"I don't." He nodded toward the amber in her palm. "But you will. You've got questions now."

She pocketed the clef. Picked up the dead phone, turned it over once, and set it back on his counter.

"Keep that for me," she said. "Until I figure it out."

She was gone before he could answer—through the door and into the morning traffic, jacket catching the wind as she turned left toward downtown. Jay picked up the phone, felt its weight. Dead and useless and worth nothing, but she'd left it like collateral. Like a promise.

He slid it into the drawer beneath the register, next to the spare keys and the [[repair toolkit]] he never used.

Three days later, she came back.

The shop was empty except for a kid browsing the synthetic pieces by the window—tourist's child, bored, dragging a finger across the glass. Jay was inventorying the back stock when the door chimed. He came out to find Tan standing at the counter, a leather satchel over her shoulder, looking at him like she'd been working through a problem and arrived at an answer she didn't quite trust.

"I owe you twelve hundred," she said.

"You do."

She reached into the satchel. Pulled out cash—actual paper bills, worn soft, bundled with a rubber band. Counted twelve hundreds onto the glass between them, her movements careful, like someone who'd learned the ritual recently and wanted to get it right.

"Someone taught you," Jay said.

"A man at the [[Temporal Adjustment Center]] on Fourteenth." She pushed the stack toward him. "He said this was the old way. That it still works everywhere."

Jay gathered the bills. "It does."

"He also said I should tip you. For being patient." She paused. "I don't know what that means here."

"It means you give extra money. For service." He tucked the bills into the register without counting them twice. "You don't have to."

"But people do?"

"Some people. When they want to."

She considered this, her hand still hovering near the satchel. The kid by the window had stopped pretending to browse and was watching them openly now—a boy, maybe ten, with the glazed patience of someone waiting for a parent to finish shopping somewhere more interesting.

"I don't know what amount," Tan said. "The man at the center said ten percent, but he also said twenty percent, and then he said it depended on things he couldn't explain."

"That's about right."

"How can both be right?"

Jay shrugged. "It's not math. It's—" He searched for the word. "Social. You're saying something about who you are, how the interaction went. Whether you want to come back."

She looked at him then, really looked, and he felt the shift in her attention like pressure against his skin. The kid by the window knocked something off its stand—a chunk of [[synthetic amber from the Phantas workshops]], harmless, worth maybe forty dollars—and Jay didn't turn to check.

"I want to come back," she said.

"Then don't tip." He pulled her phone from the drawer, set it on the counter between them. "Keep your money. Buy something next time."

She didn't pick up the phone. Instead she turned toward the window, toward the kid who was carefully replacing the piece he'd knocked over, toward the map seller still working his corner outside.

"What's the best thing you have?" she asked.

Jay didn't answer right away. He came around the counter, closer than he'd stood to her before, and moved toward the glass case against the far wall—not the one tourists browsed but a smaller cabinet half-hidden behind a display of [[Baltic Grade-A specimens]]. The kid by the window watched him pass, then looked at Tan, then at his shoes.

"Best is complicated." He unlocked the case with a key from his pocket. "Best for investment, you want certified pieces, provenance papers. Best for wearing, color and clarity. Best for keeping—that's different."

On the velvet tray he pulled out sat a piece smaller than his thumbnail. Dark amber, almost brown, with something suspended at its center that the light couldn't quite reach. Tan leaned in.

"What is that?"

"Nobody knows." He lifted it between thumb and forefinger. The thing inside was too small to identify—a fragment, a curl, a ghost of movement frozen mid-gesture. "My uncle bought this from a diver working the [[Phantas deposits off New Guinea]], thirty years before I was born. Diver said it came from deeper than the commercial layers. My uncle figured it was contamination, debris. Kept it anyway."

Tan's fingers hovered near his palm. She didn't take the piece, didn't pull back.

"Why?"

"Because he couldn't stop looking at it."

The kid's parent appeared in the doorway—a woman in clothes that cost more than Jay's rent—and the boy moved toward her without being called. The door chimed behind them.

Tan was still looking at the amber. "That's not for sale."

"No."

"Then why show me?"

Jay set it back on the velvet. "You asked what was best."

The light through the window shifted—a cloud passing, or the angle changing as morning turned. Tan straightened, her hand falling away from where it had hovered near his.

"You could have sold it," she said. "Someone would pay."

"Plenty of someones." Jay locked the case, pocketed the key. "My uncle had offers. I've had offers. Tourists, mostly. They see it back there and they know."

"Know what?"

"That it's different." He moved behind the counter, glass between them again. "Something in how it sits. They want it because they can tell I won't sell it."

Outside, the map seller was folding his table—early for him, but the crowds had thinned. Tan watched him roll the canvas tight, tuck the stand under his arm, glance toward the shop like he was checking whether Jay had noticed.

"Where I'm from, people don't keep things." She picked up the phone, turned it in her palm. "Everything moves. Value is in the moving."

"Sounds exhausting."

"It is." She set the phone back on the counter. Not toward him—just down, released. "I don't need this. It doesn't work the way I think."

"It's yours."

"Keep it for me." Her fingers tapped the glass once, a rhythm she probably didn't know she made. "I want to understand why people hold onto things."

The door chimed behind her. Jay watched her turn right this time—not downtown but west, toward the water where the [[cargo terminals]] lined the shore and cranes moved containers between eras. The phone sat on the counter like an anchor dropped.

"I know," Jay said. He took her hand.

Tan's fingers tightened around his. Relief moved across her face—the same relief she'd shown when he gave her the clef that first day, when she couldn't work the phone and he'd made the problem go away.

"We should sleep," she said. "The return window opens in six hours. I want to take the [[Rheth-7 relay]] instead of the waystation route—the currents are faster, and my father's people can start on the arbitration filings before we even clear the boundary."

She was already planning. Already moving forward, past this moment, past what had happened between them. Jay watched her pull the expedition pack toward her, checking equipment, reviewing data chips she'd collected from M-16.

He didn't feel angry anymore. That was the strange thing. The anger had burned through him for weeks—through the freight lines and the hidden platforms, through Adisa's courtyard and Yusuf's hand-drawn maps. It had kept him moving when exhaustion should have stopped him.

Now, sitting across from her in the breathing dark, he felt something else. Not peace. Clarity, maybe. The understanding that she would never see him the way he saw her. Not because she was cruel, but because the distance between them was built into the structure of their worlds.

She loved him. He believed that. She loved him the way she loved the data she'd gathered, the routes she'd mapped. Precious and fascinating and ultimately hers.

The bedroll held his shape. He lay back and closed his eyes.

Jay woke to Tan's hand on his shoulder. The walls had contracted while he slept, the passage narrower now, the light different—more amber than the pale Mystas glow he'd grown accustomed to.

"Current window's opening," she said. "Twenty minutes."

She was already packed. Her expedition cases stood in a neat row by the passage mouth, data chips secured, navigation equipment calibrated. She'd been awake for hours, he realized. Planning the route. Checking conditions. Moving forward.

Jay rolled his bedroll and stuffed it into his pack—the same pack he'd carried from Oakland, through the freight lines, through every junction and waystation. The material had worn thin at the shoulder straps. He'd need to replace it eventually.

Tan watched him struggle with the compression strap. She didn't offer to help. Not out of unkindness—she simply didn't notice he was struggling. Her attention had already moved to the [[bearing sequence]] she was reviewing on a small display, numbers scrolling in configurations Jay almost understood now.

"The relay's faster than I expected," she said. "We'll clear the boundary by midday. My father's people can have provisional clearance filed before evening."

She spoke like someone describing a solved problem. The investigation, the charges, the weeks Jay had spent running—all of it reduced to administrative details her family could handle.

The walls breathed. Jay shouldered his pack.

"Lead the way," he said.

The passage twisted as they moved through it. Jay followed Tan's expedition light, watching the walls shift from amber to something greener, the texture changing under his fingers when he steadied himself. The floor had gone soft in places—not wet, but yielding, like walking on something that hadn't decided what it wanted to be.

Tan navigated without hesitation. She checked her bearing sequence at each junction, made adjustments, continued. Twice she called back corrections—"Left here, the right passage dead-ends"—without slowing, without turning to see if he'd heard.

They passed through a narrow section where the walls pressed close enough that Jay had to turn sideways, his pack scraping against surfaces that contracted at his touch. Tan slipped through easily. Her equipment was compact, professional, designed for exactly this. His pack caught on something and he had to wrench it free.

She was twenty meters ahead before she noticed he'd stopped.

"The [[Rheth-7 intake chamber]] is just past this section," she called back. "The walls open up."

Jay worked his pack loose. The shoulder strap had torn where it caught—a clean rip through material that had already been wearing thin. He'd carried this pack from Oakland. Through the service gates and freight lines, through Adisa's courtyard, through every waystation and junction. Now it was failing.

Tan waited at the passage mouth, her light illuminating the space beyond—wider, more stable, the walls holding still.

"Ready?" she asked.

The pack hung wrong on his shoulder. Jay adjusted the remaining strap and walked toward her light.

The intake chamber opened around them like a held breath releasing. Walls of polished stone curved upward to a ceiling Jay couldn't see—lost in the amber glow that seemed to generate from the surfaces themselves. Equipment lined the far wall: charging stations, supply caches, a [[transit calibration array]] with lights blinking in sequences he recognized now from weeks of watching similar panels across a dozen waystations.

Tan moved through the space like she owned it. She probably did, in some sense—her family's sigil marked the supply caches, the charging stations, the manifest panel she was already interfacing with through her neural link. Her fingers twitched at her sides while her eyes tracked something invisible.

Jay found a bench carved into the wall and sat. His torn pack slumped beside him. The chamber was warm—warmer than anything he'd felt since leaving Oakland, a warmth that came from somewhere below, from systems humming beneath the floor.

"Relay's running twelve minutes behind schedule," Tan said, still looking at nothing. "Current interference from the M-12 junction. We'll make up time on the other side."

She hadn't asked if he needed water. Hadn't noticed the pack, the torn strap, the way he'd been favoring his left shoulder since the narrow passage. She was managing logistics. She was very good at logistics.

A chime sounded somewhere. Tan turned toward a door Jay hadn't noticed—a seam in the curved wall that was opening now, revealing a platform beyond.

"That's us," she said.

The platform extended into darkness. Not the yielding darkness of the passages, but something engineered—a space designed to hold absence until filled. Lights embedded in the floor traced a path toward a vessel anchored at the platform's edge, its hull catching the amber glow from the chamber behind them.

Tan was already moving down the path, her cases hovering on [[suspension lifts]] she'd summoned from a panel Jay hadn't seen her touch. The cases floated behind her in a neat line, following her trajectory like obedient animals.

Jay picked up his torn pack and walked.

The vessel was smaller than he'd expected. Sleek, windowless, built for function rather than comfort. Tan keyed something at its entrance and a section of hull slid aside, revealing an interior of curved seats and restraint webbing.

"Six hours to the main relay," she said, stowing her cases in compartments that opened at her approach. "You should sleep if you can. The transition through the [[boundary current]] can be disorienting."

She meant it kindly. He could hear that now—the genuine care in her voice, the desire for him to be comfortable. She wanted him to be happy. She wanted him to enjoy the journey, to appreciate the technology, to arrive rested and ready for whatever came next.

She just didn't think to ask if he was hungry. Or if his shoulder hurt. Or if he wanted to talk about any of it—the weeks of running, the body at M-11, what came after.

Jay found a seat and pulled the webbing across his chest. The restraints adjusted automatically, finding the shape of him.

The vessel hummed. Jay felt it in his chest before he heard it—a frequency that settled into his bones as the platform fell away behind them. Through the hull he could sense movement, though there was nothing to see. No windows, no displays. Just the curved interior and the amber light strips that pulsed in slow rhythm.

Tan sat across from him, her restraints configured differently than his—looser, familiar with her shape from previous journeys. She was still interfacing with something invisible, her fingers making small adjustments in the air.

"I've been thinking," she said. "About when we get back."

Jay waited.

"The [[Temporal Arbitration]] filing will take about a week to process. My father's people can expedite, but there's a sequence—provisional clearance first, then residency review, then formal dismissal of charges." Her fingers moved. "During that week, you'd stay at the household. Guest status, not dependent. It's different. More autonomy."

"And after the week?"

"That depends on what you want." She looked at him then, her eyes bright. "The Institute has a program for temporal mechanics—you'd qualify for the accelerated track, given your navigation experience. Eighteen months. After that, you could work boundary survey. The pay is good. The work is—" She smiled. "You've seen it now. You understand why I love it."

She was offering him a life. A real one, with training and purpose and a path forward. She was offering it the way she'd offered him clef that first day in Oakland—generously, easily, without understanding what it cost to receive.

"What about the shop?" Jay asked.

Tan's smile flickered. "The shop?"

"Your uncle's shop," she said, as if placing it in a catalog. "The clef business."

"Yes."

The vessel's hum shifted pitch as they passed through something—a current junction, maybe, or a boundary marker. Tan's fingers paused in the air.

"I don't understand the question," she said. "You've been gone for—" She calculated. "Subjectively, almost three months. Objectively, years in that timeframe. The shop isn't waiting for you. Nothing waits."

"I know."

"So what about it?"

Jay watched the amber light pulse along the wall. Slow rhythm, steady. The [[Rheth Extraction Consortium]] built their vessels to soothe, he realized. To make passengers forget they were hurtling through dimensions that would tear them apart without the hull's protection.

"I want to go back to it," he said. "Whatever's left. Whatever it's become."

Tan's confusion wasn't performed. He could see her genuinely trying to understand, running through possibilities the way she'd run through current calculations at the M-15 junction. Her mind was brilliant at navigation, at logistics, at solving problems that had solutions.

"You could sell clef anywhere," she said finally. "Here, even. There's a market. Luxury goods from temporal sources, authenticated provenance—you have expertise. I could introduce you to the right people."

"That's not—"

"Or if it's about the location specifically, we could arrange visits. Regular transit. You'd have access once your status is formalized."

She was trying. That was the thing that sat heaviest in his chest. She was trying so hard to give him what he wanted, and she couldn't see the shape of it.

"That's not what I mean." The words came harder than they should have. Weeks of running had worn something down in him—the part that used to translate easily between what he felt and what he said. "The shop isn't a job. It's not about selling things."

Tan waited. Her hands had stilled, no longer making adjustments to invisible systems. She was listening. Really listening, in the way she had those first nights in Oakland when she'd sat on the crate behind his counter and asked him to explain layaway.

"My uncle held that amber every night for thirty years," Jay said. "The piece from the [[Phantas Drift deposits]]. He didn't hold it because it was valuable. He held it because it was his. Because he'd chosen it, and kept choosing it, and that choosing was who he was."

The vessel's hum dropped into a lower register. A junction, maybe. Or they were slowing for something.

"I understand," Tan said.

But he could see that she didn't. She understood the words—attachment, inheritance, continuity. She could define them, contextualize them, place them in a framework of temporal psychology and cultural adaptation. What she couldn't do was feel why a narrow storefront between a nail salon and a bodega might be worth more than everything she was offering.

"If you went back," she said carefully, "you'd be giving up—" She stopped, recalculated. "I'm not saying you shouldn't. I'm trying to understand what you'd be going back *to*."

"Home," Jay said.

The word sat between them. Tan's expression shifted—not quite a flinch, but something close. As if he'd named a destination she didn't have coordinates for.

"Home," Tan repeated. She said it the way she'd said *layaway* that first week in Oakland—testing its weight, trying to find where it fit in her understanding. "You mean the specific coordinates. The temporal location where you—"

"No." Jay shifted in his restraints. The vessel's soothing hum had started to feel less like comfort and more like pressure. "I mean the place I chose. The life I was building."

Tan was quiet for a long moment. Outside the hull—if there was an outside—currents moved in directions he couldn't name. She was thinking, he knew. Running calculations. Looking for a solution the way she'd looked for solutions at every junction since he'd found her at M-15.

"What if we found you something similar?" she said finally. "A space. In a [[temporal commerce district]]—there's one near the household, actually. You could curate pieces, build a clientele. I know people who collect era-specific artifacts. The provenance you have, the knowledge—"

"Tan."

"—you'd have full autonomy. I wouldn't be your sponsor; we could arrange independent status through my father's—"

"Tan."

She stopped.

The amber light pulsed. Once, twice. Jay watched her face—the small movements around her eyes as she processed the fact that he'd interrupted her, that the solution she was building wasn't landing.

"You're not hearing me," he said.

"I'm trying." And she was. He could see the effort, the genuine attention she was bringing to the problem of him. But that was exactly it. He was a problem to be solved. A navigational challenge with variables she needed to adjust.

"Are you?" he asked.

The vessel shuddered—a current junction, or maybe just turbulence in unmapped space. Tan's hands moved reflexively, checking systems he couldn't see.

The turbulence passed. Tan's hands settled. But she didn't answer his question—not directly. Instead, she turned slightly in her restraints, and when she spoke, her voice had the careful patience of someone explaining [[current navigation fundamentals]] to a trainee.

"I hear that you want to go back. I understand that. What I'm trying to help you see is that 'back' isn't a fixed point. The Oakland you left has already changed. It will keep changing. The shop—"

"Is mine."

"—was yours. And it can be again, in some form. But clinging to a specific configuration of walls and inventory when you could have—" She gestured at the hull around them, at whatever lay beyond it. "This is what I don't understand. Why limit yourself?"

Jay watched her face. She meant it. Every word. She genuinely believed she was offering him more, better, larger. And she couldn't see—would never see—that the narrowness was the point. That his uncle had chosen twelve feet of Telegraph Avenue and held it for thirty years not because he couldn't imagine anything else, but because he didn't want anything else.

"You're not trying to understand," Jay said quietly. "You're trying to solve me."

Tan's expression flickered—something that might have been hurt, or might have been frustration, or might have been the particular confusion of someone who'd never failed to solve a problem before.

"That's not fair."

"No," Jay agreed. "It isn't."

The vessel's hum shifted again. Through the amber light, Jay could see the shape of what came next: she would keep trying, keep offering, keep solving. And every solution would require him to become someone she could understand. Someone legible. Someone less.

She could ask. She could say: *What do you want?* and actually wait for the answer. But even as Jay watched her, he knew she wouldn't. The question itself would require her to step into a space where she wasn't the one with the map.

The vessel's amber light shifted—brighter now, steadier. Through the hull, he could feel the currents smoothing. They were approaching the relay.

"When we dock," Tan said, "I'll have my father's people meet us. The legal processing can start immediately. If you want to wait before deciding about the Institute—"

"I'm not going to the Institute."

"—we can defer enrollment until you've had time to—"

"Tan."

She stopped. The light caught her face at an angle that made her look younger than she was—or older, maybe. Someone who'd never had to hold onto anything because everything had always been available.

"I'm going back to Oakland," Jay said.

She nodded slowly. Not agreement—processing. Running the variables, looking for the place where the problem resolved.

"The charges will take time to clear," she said. "Even with my father's intervention. You'd be returning to active investigation."

"I know."

"And the shop—" She hesitated. "It won't be what you remember."

"I know."

The vessel shuddered once, then settled into a deeper hum. Docking sequence. Outside, the [[Rheth-7 main relay]] would be waiting—transit platforms and commerce wings and the long routes back to every mapped time.

Tan looked at him. For a moment, he thought she might say something real—not a solution, not an offer, just something true about what they'd been to each other.

"I hope you find what you're looking for," she said.

And Jay understood that this was goodbye.

The docking seal released with a sound like held breath. Jay unbuckled his restraints and stood in the amber light, feeling the vessel's hum fade from his bones.

Tan didn't move from her seat. She was already somewhere else—interface-deep, probably coordinating with her father's people about the legal filings. About him. The problem she hadn't solved.

Jay shouldered his torn pack and stepped through the threshold.

The Rheth-7 main relay opened around him in tiers of polished transit platforms, each one marked with route designations in scripts he'd learned to read during his weeks in the margins. [[Primas Mainline]] gates dominated the central axis, their departure boards cycling through temporal coordinates. Smaller passages branched toward Phantas routes and, at the far edges where fewer travelers gathered, the Mystas corridors he'd navigated with Yusuf.

His tag pulsed once—still active, still marking him as Tan's dependent. That would complicate things. The charges, the investigation, the questions about where he'd been and how he'd traveled. Her father's lawyers might clear the murder suspicion, but they'd want to know about the underground routes, the freight lines, the people who'd moved him through unmonitored space.

Jay found a commissary alcove and ordered water. The panel accepted his tag without hesitation—full integration now, for whatever that was worth.

Across the platform, a woman in worn gray watched him. She had the look of someone who worked the margins: alert, unhurried, professionally invisible. When their eyes met, she didn't look away. Instead, she touched her wrist—the same gesture Callum had used in Sector Nine.

Jay's debt to Adisa was still on the ledger. Sixteen hours, plus whatever interest had accrued.

The woman crossed the platform without hurrying. Up close, she was older than he'd first thought—forty, maybe fifty, with the kind of face that had learned not to show its calculations.

"You're the one Adisa moved through Vostok," she said. Not a question.

"The debt transferred."

"Debts always transfer." She glanced at his torn pack, at the tag pulsing faintly on his wrist. "Sixteen hours won't clear what you owe. Not anymore."

Jay felt the relay's currents shifting beneath the platform—departures cycling, arrivals humming through the gates. Somewhere behind him, the vessel that had carried him from the edges was already preparing for its next run.

"What changed?"

"You did." The woman produced a thin card from her sleeve—blank on one side, marked on the other with a sequence of symbols he'd learned to read in the freight corridors. "Solo routing through unmapped Mystas. Return transit from beyond M-15. That kind of movement gets noticed. People want to know who trained you."

"No one trained me."

Her expression didn't change, but something shifted behind her eyes—reassessment, maybe. Interest.

"Then they'll want to know how." She held out the card. "Adisa says your hours are flexible. Work them off her way, or work them off ours. Either way, the ledger clears."

The symbols on the card resolved into coordinates—not a destination but a routing instruction. [[Sublateral Junction Twelve]], if he was reading it right. Deep in the network, far from monitored space.

"What's the work?"

"Someone needs moving," she said. "Someone who can't use the gates."

Jay turned the card in his fingers. The symbols were precise—junction number, approach vector, a timing window that started in three hours.

"Moving people through unmapped routes is what got me accused of murder."

"You weren't accused of moving people. You were accused of making someone disappear." The woman's gaze didn't waver. "Different skill set. The first one pays. The second one gets you investigated."

Behind her, a family crossed the platform toward the Primas gates—two adults, a child, all of them moving with the easy confidence of people whose tags opened every door. The child was laughing at something only she could see through her interface.

"Who needs moving?"

"A woman. Origin time roughly two centuries back from yours. She overstayed a labor contract in the [[Phantas industrial zones]]—mining work, the kind that wears bodies down faster than the documentation admits. Her sponsor filed abandonment charges when she stopped reporting. Now she's stuck in a transit hub three junctions from here with no tag and patrol cycling through every six hours."

Jay thought of the woman in the future commons, the one with the worn bracelet who'd directed him to Callum. The way she'd looked at him—recognizing something, maybe. A shared position.

"What happens if she's caught?"

"Forced return. Which sounds neutral until you understand what two centuries of temporal displacement does to a body that's already damaged." The woman watched him process this. "She has maybe thirty hours before the patrol patterns tighten. After that, the windows close."

The card felt heavier than it should.

"Three hours," Jay said.

"Platform Nine. Service corridor behind the maintenance alcove." She was already turning away. "Don't be late."

Jay found Platform Nine at the relay's eastern edge, where the polished transit surfaces gave way to utilitarian gray. The maintenance alcove was marked with symbols he wouldn't have recognized three months ago—routing notation, the underground's private language.

The service corridor behind it smelled of recycled air and old metal. Emergency lighting cast everything in amber strips that reminded him of the shop, of sunlight through the front window hitting rows of clef in their cases. He pushed the thought away.

The woman from the platform was waiting at the first junction. She handed him a second card—different symbols this time, a route that wound through [[Sublateral Junction Twelve]] and then deeper, into passages he'd need the bearing finder for.

"Her name is Sera," the woman said. "She won't trust you. Don't take it personally."

"How do I find her?"

"Transit hub at Junction Seven. She's been sleeping in a cargo hold behind the secondary freight platform—the one they use for equipment transfers to the [[Phantas industrial zones]]. She knows you're coming. Show her the card and give her this." She pressed something small into Jay's palm: a ration packet with a symbol scratched into the wrapper. "She'll know what it means."

Jay looked at the packet. The symbol was the same one Adisa had worn on her sleeve—a mark of the network, recognizable to those who needed to recognize it.

"And if patrol finds us?"

"Then you learn how fast you can move through unmapped space." The woman was already backing into the shadows. "You made it from M-15. This should be easy."

It wasn't a compliment. It was a calculation.

The sublateral network opened differently than the Mystas passages—wider, with more stable footing, but also older. The walls here had been carved by decades of use, surfaces worn smooth by hands finding purchase in the dark. Jay followed the bearing finder's steady pulse, counting junctions the way Yusuf had taught him.

Junction Twelve was a convergence point, six corridors meeting in a chamber lit by emergency strips that flickered on a four-second cycle. Someone had scratched route markers into the stone at knee height—the underground's language again, directions for people who couldn't afford to be lost.

He took the second corridor, angling toward the freight platforms.

The air changed as he descended. Warmer, tinged with something chemical—lubricant, maybe, or the residue from whatever they shipped through the [[Phantas industrial zones]]. The secondary freight platform announced itself through sound before sight: the low hum of equipment in standby mode, the intermittent clank of cargo containers shifting on their rails.

The hold was exactly where the woman had described it. A gap between two massive shipping units, barely wide enough to squeeze through. Inside, the space opened into a makeshift shelter—blankets arranged on flattened packaging material, a water container rigged to catch condensation from an overhead pipe, and a woman pressed against the far wall with her hands raised and her eyes tracking every movement Jay made.

She was older than he'd expected. Sixty, maybe more—though temporal displacement made age hard to read. Her fingers were scarred in patterns he recognized from the equipment manifests Adisa had shown him. Mining damage.

"Adisa's network," Jay said, and held out the ration packet.

Sera's eyes went to the packet first, then to the symbol scratched into the wrapper. Her hands lowered slowly, but she didn't move from the wall.

"You're not what I expected."

Jay stayed where he was, the gap between them maybe six feet of stacked packaging and condensation-damp air. "What did you expect?"

"Someone who knew what they were doing." Her voice was rough, accented in ways Jay couldn't place—two centuries was a long time for language to drift. "You're holding the packet like it might bite you."

He looked down. She was right; his grip had gone white-knuckled without him noticing. He set the packet on the nearest flat surface and stepped back.

"I've done this route before. Different direction."

"Running from something." It wasn't a question. Sera's scarred hands moved to her sides, and Jay saw the way her fingers curled—protective, favoring the joints. The [[Phantas extraction protocols]] hadn't been designed for bodies that needed to last. "You have that look. The one that says you're still surprised anyone would help you."

"Someone helped you."

"Someone took payment." She reached for the ration packet, tore it open with practiced efficiency. "Twelve years of labor debt, transferred to people who don't file paperwork. That's not help. That's a different kind of ownership."

She ate in small, careful bites. Jay watched the emergency strips cycle through their four-second pattern and thought about the woman on the platform, the calculation in her voice when she'd said *you made it from M-15*.

"We have six hours before patrol cycles back," he said. "Can you walk?"

"I can walk." Sera pushed herself up from the wall, and Jay saw what that cost her—the way her weight shifted to favor her left side, the pause before each movement as if she had to convince her body to cooperate. "I walked twelve years in those tunnels. I can walk out of this."

She moved past him toward the gap in the cargo containers, and he noticed she'd already packed. A single bag, smaller than his had been when he left Oakland. Everything she owned in a space that could fit under a transit seat.

The secondary platform was quiet when they emerged. Jay checked the bearing finder—pulse steady, route clear. Four hours and forty minutes until patrol cycle.

"This way."

They moved through the freight area in silence, Sera's footsteps careful on the metal grating. At the service corridor entrance, she stopped.

"The woman who sent you. She told you what happens if they catch me."

"Forced return."

"That's what the paperwork calls it." Sera's scarred hands found the corridor wall, steadying herself for the descent. "My body remembers the [[Phantas Drift deposits]]. The pressure, the cold. Two centuries of medical difference between where I'm from and where they'd send me back to." She looked at him directly for the first time. "I'd have maybe a week. Less if the return displacement hits hard."

Jay thought about Tan navigating the Mystas passages, never once checking if he could keep up.

"I know the route," he said. "Stay close."

He started down the corridor, and after a moment, he heard her following.

The service corridor narrowed after the first junction, walls pressing close enough that they had to move single file. Jay kept his pace slower than he would have alone, listening for Sera's footsteps behind him.

"You learned this route running," she said. Not accusatory. Observational, the way someone notes weather.

"Different route. Same principle."

"And now you're on the other side of it." Her breathing had changed—heavier, with a catch on the exhale. "Funny how that works."

Jay stopped at a maintenance alcove, checking the bearing finder. The pulse had shifted slightly—someone had moved cargo through the main artery, changing the network's pressure. They'd need to detour through the [[secondary Primas junction]] to avoid crossing paths with whatever crew was working the freight lines.

"We rest here. Two minutes."

Sera lowered herself onto a pipe housing, her scarred hands gripping the metal for balance. In the dim emergency lighting, Jay could see the way the mining damage had reshaped her joints—knuckles swollen, fingers bent at angles that didn't quite match.

"You keep looking at my hands."

"Sorry."

"Don't be." She flexed them, a practiced motion. "They look worse than they work. Twelve years teaches you which pain matters and which is just noise." She studied him the way he'd been studying her. "You're young for this work. Young for that look you carry."

"What look?"

"The one that says someone showed you exactly how much you didn't matter to them." She pushed herself up before he could respond. "Two minutes is over. Which way?"

The secondary Primas junction opened into a broader space—a hub where freight routes crossed before splitting toward different temporal destinations. Jay counted the corridor mouths the way Yusuf had taught him. Third from the left, marked with a scratch pattern that looked accidental if you didn't know what to look for.

"Through there. Forty minutes to the next rest point."

Sera moved past him, and he noticed she'd found her rhythm now—still favoring her left side, but the pauses between movements had shortened. Twelve years in the tunnels had taught her how to calibrate effort, to ration what her body could give.

The corridor beyond the junction was warmer, pipes running along the ceiling carrying something that hummed with heat. Jay felt sweat prickle along his spine.

"The [[thermal routing systems]]," Sera said behind him. "They run hot cargo through here. Temperature-sensitive materials moving between eras." A pause in her footsteps. "I loaded those shipments for three years. Before they moved me to the pressure work."

"What kind of cargo?"

"Medical compounds, mostly. Things that don't exist yet in some eras. Don't exist anymore in others." Her voice carried the flatness of someone describing weather. "The margins on temporal pharmaceuticals—you wouldn't believe what people pay to bring medicine backward. Or forward, if their own time stopped making it."

Jay thought about the clef tourists buying in his shop. The casual wealth of people who could afford to visit 2025 for entertainment.

"I'd believe it."

Sera made a sound that might have been a laugh. "Maybe you would."

They walked in silence for a while, the heat building around them. Jay's shirt stuck to his back. Sera seemed unbothered—twelve years in pressure tunnels had probably recalibrated what counted as discomfort.

At the next junction, she stopped. Not from exhaustion this time. She was studying the scratch marks on the wall, the routing symbols that Jay had learned to read during his flight from the charges.

"You learned this system fast," she said. "Faster than most."

"I had good teachers."

"No." She traced one of the symbols with a scarred finger. "This notation—it's [[Waystation Echo-Provisional]] standard. The crews who work past M-8. I've seen maybe a dozen people who can read it, and half of them never came back from the edges." She turned to face him. "Adisa's network doesn't train people in deep Mystas routing. So where did you learn?"

Jay thought about Yusuf's hand-drawn maps. The scratched markers Tan had left through unmapped passages. The body at M-11 that he'd stepped around without stopping.

"I went looking for someone."

"Did you find them?"

"Yes."

Sera waited, but he didn't elaborate. After a moment, she nodded—the nod of someone who understood that some stories stayed private.

"Thirty-two minutes to the rest point," he said.

"I know." She moved past him into the corridor. "I can read the routing too. Different system, different era, but the logic's the same." She glanced back. "You're not the only one who learned things the hard way."

The nail salon opened at eight, same as it had since 1993. Mrs. Chen arrived at seven to unlock the gate, disable the alarm, check that nothing had walked off overnight. The neighborhood had changed in thirty years—storefronts cycling through owners, languages shifting on the signs, money flowing in from directions she'd stopped trying to track—but the routine held.

She made tea in the back room while the lights warmed. The acetone smell had long since become invisible to her, part of the air itself. Her daughter Emily would arrive at seven-thirty, complaining about the bus, about her knees, about the tourists who didn't tip. Mrs. Chen would listen without responding. There was nothing to say that she hadn't said a hundred times before.

The first appointment was a woman from one of the futures—Mrs. Chen could always tell by the hands. Too smooth. The cuticles almost synthetic. This one wanted something called temporal gradient, a polish that shifted color in different light. Mrs. Chen had it. [[The supplier on International]] brought things like that, products from times she'd never visit, sold through back channels she didn't ask about.

"Left hand first," Mrs. Chen said.

The woman's fingers were cold, thin-skinned, the veins visible like ink beneath tissue paper. She wore a ring that looked like silver but weighed nothing when Mrs. Chen moved it aside.

Through the window, she could see the gate still down on Jay's shop. He usually opened around nine. She'd known him since he was a teenager, before his uncle passed, before the neighborhood became whatever it was becoming. Before the futures arrived and started buying up everything that held still long enough to price.

The woman didn't make small talk. Most of them didn't. They watched their devices—thin sheets of something that wasn't quite glass, held loosely or propped against their bags—or they stared at nothing, eyes moving in patterns Mrs. Chen had learned meant they were seeing something she couldn't. Neural interfaces, Emily had explained once. Like phones in their heads.

Mrs. Chen worked the cuticles with practiced pressure. Thirty years of hands. Hands that shook, hands covered in calluses, soft hands, scarred hands, hands that flinched at the slightest touch. These future hands were always the same—maintained, preserved, like furniture under plastic.

The bell chimed. Emily came in sideways through the door, shoulder holding it open while she maneuvered a tray of coffees. "Bus was twenty minutes late," she said, not quite to anyone. "Something about the 51 line again."

Mrs. Chen didn't look up. The gradient polish required thin coats, each one dried before the next. Under the salon lights it looked violet. It would shift to copper in daylight, then something Emily called [[infrared bloom]]—visible only to certain implants, apparently. A color Mrs. Chen would never see.

"Morning," Emily said to the customer, setting one coffee by her mother's station. The customer didn't respond. Emily's mouth tightened, but she moved to the back without comment.

The salon filled with the sound of Emily prepping her station, the hum of the dryer, the distant bass of someone's music bleeding through the shared wall from [[the restaurant that used to be a laundromat]]. Mrs. Chen painted another coat. The woman's ring caught the light, throwing no reflection at all.

The woman finished without speaking. Payment came through whatever invisible system they used—Mrs. Chen's reader buzzed, showed a number, and she accepted it without understanding where the money came from or where it went. The tip was exactly fifteen percent. It always was, with them. Not generous, not insulting. Calculated.

"Come back anytime," Mrs. Chen said. The words were automatic.

The woman left, the door chime marking her exit. Through the window, Mrs. Chen watched her walk past Jay's shop—gate still down—and turn toward [[the pickup zone on 40th]], where the private transports waited for people who didn't take buses.

Emily emerged from the back, coffee in hand. "She tip?"

"Fifteen percent."

"Always." Emily sat at her station, scrolling through her phone. Real phone, real glass, real fingers on the screen. Mrs. Chen found comfort in that. "Mrs. Delgado called. Rescheduling to Thursday. Said [[the development group]] bought the building next to hers."

"Which one?"

"She didn't catch the name. Some futures holding company. They're all the same."

Mrs. Chen cleaned her station, laid out fresh towels. The morning light had shifted, Jay's gate still down across the street. That wasn't like him. She thought about walking over, but her nine o'clock would be here soon—Mrs. Patterson, same French tips for twelve years, same conversation about her grandchildren. Some things held.

The acetone smell had become visible again, sharp in her nose. That happened sometimes, when she thought too hard about what was changing and what wasn't.

Mrs. Patterson came through the door at nine exactly, same as every Tuesday. Same purse, same sweater despite the weather, same smile that showed the gap between her front teeth.

"Morning, Helen." Only Mrs. Patterson called her Helen. "You see that sign they put up on the corner? The one about the new development?"

Mrs. Chen gestured to the chair. "French tips?"

"Same as always." Mrs. Patterson settled in, arranging herself the way she had for twelve years. "They're calling it [[the Temporal Quarter]]. Like we need a name for our own neighborhood."

Through the window, Mrs. Chen could see a group of tourists gathering near Jay's shop. Three of them, standing too close together, pointing at things. One held up something that might have been a camera or might have been nothing at all. They were taking pictures of the gate. Of the darkness behind it.

"My granddaughter says property values are up forty percent," Mrs. Patterson continued. "She works in real estate now. Did I tell you? Good job, benefits, the whole thing."

Mrs. Chen shaped the first nail, filed it square the way Mrs. Patterson liked. The tourists moved on, drifting toward the coffee shop that had replaced the bodega last spring. The bodega owner had sold to a holding company from somewhere in the twenty-third century—Emily had looked it up, found the registration, showed Mrs. Chen numbers that meant nothing to her.

"She says I should sell the house," Mrs. Patterson said. "Move somewhere quieter. But where would I go?"

Mrs. Chen applied the first coat of white to the nail tip. She didn't have an answer. She'd stopped having answers years ago.

"Forty-three years in that house," Mrs. Patterson said. "Richard and I bought it when the neighborhood was different. Before all this."

Mrs. Chen didn't ask what "this" meant. She knew. The tourists with their invisible devices. The shops changing hands to buyers who wouldn't arrive for centuries. The way her own rent had tripled in five years, each increase delivered by a different property management company with addresses that didn't exist yet.

She finished the white tips, moved to the clear coat. Mrs. Patterson's hands were familiar—the slight tremor in the left, the scar on her thumb from a gardening accident she'd described once, years ago. Real hands. Hands that showed their age.

"Emily," Mrs. Chen called toward the back. "Mrs. Patterson's granddaughter. The real estate job."

Emily appeared in the doorway, phone in hand. "The one at [[Meridian Properties]]?"

"That's her," Mrs. Patterson said, brightening. "You know her?"

"We went to middle school together." Emily leaned against the doorframe. "She's doing the temporal assessments now. Figuring out which buildings are worth buying across which eras."

Mrs. Patterson's face did something complicated. Pride and something else, something she tucked away quickly. "She always was good with numbers."

Mrs. Chen applied the final coat, watching the clear polish settle into the familiar shape of French tips. Same as twelve years ago. Same as next Tuesday. Outside, a transport lifted silently from the pickup zone, carrying someone back to a time Mrs. Chen would never see.

The acetone smell faded. The morning continued.

Mrs. Patterson paid in cash—always had, always would. Bills worn soft at the edges, exact change counted out on the counter. She pressed a five-dollar tip into Mrs. Chen's palm the way she'd done for twelve years, hand over hand, like passing a secret.

"You take care, Helen." The door chime marked her leaving.

Through the window, Mrs. Chen watched her walk toward the bus stop. Mrs. Patterson still took the bus. Still lived in the same house. Still came every Tuesday. Some people held on like that. Others sold and disappeared into numbers on a screen.

"Her granddaughter tried to recruit me last month," Emily said from her station. She wasn't looking at her phone anymore. "Meridian. Part of their [[local sourcing initiative]]—they need people who actually grew up here. 'Historical context,' she called it."

Mrs. Chen cleaned her tools, laid them in the sterilization tray. She didn't ask the question.

"I told her no." Emily's voice had an edge Mrs. Chen recognized—defensive before being accused. "I'm not helping them figure out which buildings to buy."

The sterilization tray hummed. Across the street, Jay's gate stayed down. Mrs. Chen checked the time: 10:14. His shop should have opened two hours ago. She thought about the tourists photographing the darkness behind the iron, the way they'd moved on without concern. To them it was just another closed shop, another piece of the scenery.

"Something's wrong over there," Emily said, following her gaze. "He's never closed this late. Not even when [[his uncle was in the hospital]]."

Mrs. Chen wiped down her station. The acetone smell had returned, sharp and familiar. She was already reaching for her keys.

pages.content:
Emily caught her arm before she reached the door. "Mom. What are you doing?"

"Looking." Mrs. Chen pulled free, gentler than the motion suggested. "Watch the shop."

The street was bright and warm, the kind of October morning that didn't feel like October anymore. Mrs. Chen crossed without waiting for the light—she'd been crossing this street for thirty-two years, knew its rhythms better than any signal. A transport hummed past, close enough to stir her hair.

Jay's gate was solid iron, painted black, the paint flaking at the bottom where weather got to it. Through the gaps she could see the shop's interior: dim shapes of shelves, the counter where she'd bought clef once out of curiosity, the back door that led to his apartment upstairs. Everything still. Everything dark.

She tried the gate. Locked. She pressed her face closer, cupping her hands around her eyes.

The cash drawer was open. Not pulled out, just—open. Like someone had been interrupted.

"Mom." Emily had followed her, was standing too close. "We should call someone."

"Who?" Mrs. Chen didn't turn around. "[[The temporal authority]]? The police? You think they'll come for a closed shop?"

"Then what are we supposed to do?"

Mrs. Chen stepped back from the gate. A tourist couple passed behind them, speaking a language that didn't exist yet, not looking at the closed shop or the two women standing before it. Just scenery. Background for their photographs.

"We wait," Mrs. Chen said. "We watch."

She walked back to her salon. The door chime rang. The acetone smell wrapped around her like something she could hold.

The morning settled back into itself. Mrs. Delgado arrived at 10:30, her usual appointment, acrylics with the pale coral tips she'd been getting since her son's engagement. She talked about the wedding venue in Alameda, the caterer who wanted to source ingredients from agricultural futures, how her mother-in-law kept insisting on chrysanthemums even though they weren't in season anywhere she recognized.

Mrs. Chen worked the acrylic powder, mixed the liquid, built the shape one layer at a time. Her hands knew this motion. Through the window she could see Jay's gate in her peripheral vision—still down, the morning light making the peeling paint more visible.

Emily hadn't gone back to her phone. She was watching the street, arms crossed over her chest, and Mrs. Chen recognized the posture from when Emily was fourteen and fighting something she couldn't name.

"You know people," Mrs. Chen said. It wasn't a question.

"I know people." Emily uncrossed her arms. "There's a [[neighborhood signal group]]—people who actually live here, not the tourist channels. Someone posted about Jay this morning. Asking if anyone's seen him."

Mrs. Delgado looked up, interested. Mrs. Chen kept her eyes on the acrylic.

"Three days," Emily said. "That's what people are saying. No one's seen him in three days."

The acrylic hardened under Mrs. Chen's file. Three days. The cash drawer open. The tourists photographing a mystery they'd move on from in minutes.

"The wedding's in March," Mrs. Delgado said, filling the silence. "If you want to come. You've done my nails for so long."

Mrs. Chen smiled. Filed. Watched Emily pull up something on her phone, face tight with the kind of purpose that looked too much like her father.

Mrs. Delgado left at eleven, coral tips gleaming under the overhead lights. Mrs. Chen cleaned her station, emptied the acetone dish, arranged her tools in their familiar positions. The rhythm of it steadied her hands.

"Someone's organizing a check-in." Emily's voice was flat, reading. "Going door to door on his building. They want to know if anyone has a key, or knows his [[emergency contacts]]."

"His uncle's gone." Mrs. Chen wiped down the counter. "I don't know who else."

"There was a woman. People saw her around his shop for a few weeks before—" Emily stopped. "You must have seen her too."

Mrs. Chen had seen her. Smooth hands, expensive clothes that tried not to look expensive, the way she'd held herself like someone unaccustomed to waiting. She'd watched the woman lean against Jay's counter, laughing at something he said, and she'd thought what she always thought when she saw those pairings: be careful. Not a judgment. Just the knowledge of what happened when different times collided in the same body.

"She stopped coming," Mrs. Chen said. "Before he closed."

Emily stood up from her station. "I'm going to the check-in. If they need someone who knows the building—"

"You don't know the building."

"I know people who do." Emily grabbed her jacket from the hook by the door. The motion was sharp, decisive, everything Mrs. Chen had taught her not to be in a world that punished standing out. "Someone has to do something besides wait."

The door chimed. Mrs. Chen watched her daughter cross the street toward the small crowd gathering at Jay's gate. She counted three tourists among them, filming.

The salon was quiet in the way it got between appointments—not empty, just waiting. Mrs. Chen's noon customer wouldn't arrive for another forty minutes. She could see the crowd at Jay's gate from her station, maybe a dozen people now, Emily's jacket visible among them. Someone had brought a [[clipboard from the tenant association]], passing it around. The tourists had drifted away, found something newer to photograph.

Mrs. Chen opened her supply drawer. The temporal gradient polishes sat in their row, unlabeled bottles from the supplier on International. She'd never asked where he got them. Never asked what century made them, what hands had mixed the pigments that shifted through spectrums her eyes couldn't fully see. She'd learned early that questions were a luxury in a business where margins meant survival.

The drawer below held her regular polishes—OPI, Essie, the brands she'd stocked since 1993. The bottles were dusty. No one asked for them anymore. Even Mrs. Patterson, faithful Mrs. Patterson with her French tips, had started eyeing the gradient colors. *My granddaughter says they're quite safe*, she'd mentioned last week. *Completely integrated into the market now.*

Outside, Emily was talking to a man Mrs. Chen didn't recognize—older, gray beard, carrying what looked like a [[locksmith's kit]]. He gestured at Jay's gate. Emily nodded, her hands moving the way they did when she was explaining something she thought was obvious.

Mrs. Chen closed the drawer. The gradient polishes clinked softly against each other, catching light that hadn't existed when she'd learned this trade.

The locksmith worked quickly. Mrs. Chen could see that much from her station—the way his hands moved with the certainty of someone who'd opened a thousand locks, legal or otherwise. Emily stood beside him, holding something, maybe a flashlight, maybe just her phone.

The gate began to rise.

Mrs. Chen found herself standing, though she didn't remember deciding to. Her hands were still damp from the acetone wipe. The noon light fell across her floor in the same pattern it had fallen every day since she'd bought the lease in '93—the angle shifting with the seasons, but the shape familiar. She knew this floor. Knew the scuff marks near the door where clients shuffled their feet, the slight discoloration under her station where she'd spilled developer twelve years ago.

Through her window, she watched the darkness inside Jay's shop become visible. The gate rose in jerks, catching on something, then releasing. Emily crouched to look inside before it was fully up, and Mrs. Chen thought: *that's her father in her, that rushing forward*.

The crowd had grown again. She counted Mrs. Delgado's nephew, the woman who ran the [[alterations shop]] two doors down, faces she recognized from years of peripheral attention. No tourists now. Just neighbors, standing in the street like they used to before the futures made sidewalks into stages.

Mrs. Chen's hand was on her door before she understood she'd crossed the salon. The chime sounded behind her, high and thin, as she stepped outside for the first time since opening.

The street felt different underfoot. Not physically—same cracked asphalt, same faded crosswalk she'd been looking at for thirty years—but the act of standing in it changed something. Mrs. Chen was aware of her body in a way she usually wasn't: her hands still smelling of acetone, her knees stiff from the morning's work, the slight ache in her lower back that had become so familiar she'd stopped noticing it.

Emily saw her coming and said nothing. Just made space.

The inside of Jay's shop was darker than it should have been. The overhead lights were off, but even the daylight coming through the open gate seemed to stop at the threshold, absorbed by the cluttered shelves. Mrs. Chen could see shapes—the glass cases where he kept the clef, the old register his uncle had used, the [[back room curtain]] hanging crooked like someone had pushed through it in a hurry.

"Cash drawer's open," the locksmith said. He wasn't looking at it. He was looking at the floor near the counter, where something had been spilled and dried. Not blood—too pale, almost iridescent in the thin light that reached it. Mrs. Chen recognized the sheen. She had bottles of that sheen in her own drawer.

"That's gradient base," she heard herself say. "The solvent they use to mix temporal pigments."

Everyone turned to look at her.

Emily's expression was the worst part. Not surprise—something closer to recognition, like a piece had clicked into place that her daughter had been waiting for.

Mrs. Chen felt the weight of their attention like humidity—pressing, inescapable. She'd spent thirty years making herself small in this neighborhood, useful but unremarkable, the kind of person people forgot to wonder about.

"You know what this is?" The locksmith's voice was careful, neutral.

"I use it." She didn't elaborate. Didn't explain the supplier on International, the unlabeled bottles, the questions she'd trained herself not to ask. Emily would understand what she wasn't saying. Emily always did.

The locksmith stepped aside, and Mrs. Chen found herself moving forward into Jay's shop without deciding to. The threshold felt wrong—not dangerous, just different, like stepping into someone else's dream of a familiar room. The clef in the display cases caught light they shouldn't have been able to catch, their surfaces shimmering with that same temporal iridescence as the spilled solvent.

Jay kept his supplier records in the back. Mrs. Chen knew this because she'd asked him once, years ago, when her own supplier had raised prices and she'd wondered if there were alternatives. Jay had shown her the curtain, the [[filing cabinet]] behind it, the paper ledger he kept because digital records could be accessed, deleted, subpoenaed.

"There might be something in the back," she said. Her voice sounded strange in the shop's dead air. "He kept records. Paper ones."

Emily was already moving toward the curtain. Mrs. Chen watched her daughter's hand reach for the fabric and thought about all the things she'd never asked—about the [[products that crossed centuries]] to reach her drawer, about where they came from and who they'd belonged to before they belonged to her.

The curtain made a sound when Emily pushed through—a dry whisper, fabric against fabric, the kind of nothing-noise Mrs. Chen had heard a thousand times in her own salon. Behind it, the back room was smaller than she'd expected. A folding table cluttered with packaging materials. Cardboard boxes stacked against one wall, some open, some sealed with tape that had yellowed with age. And the filing cabinet, olive green, three drawers, the kind you could buy at any office supply store for fifty dollars.

The top drawer hung open six inches. Empty file tabs stuck up like broken teeth.

"Someone cleaned it out," Emily said.

Mrs. Chen moved past her daughter and pulled the drawer fully open. Nothing. The second drawer—nothing. The third held a [[repair manual]] for equipment she didn't recognize, diagrams showing something that looked like it belonged inside a clock, and beneath that, a single receipt.

She knew the address printed at the top. 4847 International Boulevard, Suite C. No business name. Just the address, and below it, a list: gradient base (5L), temporal stabilizer (2L), pigment concentrate—violet spectrum (500mL).

The same address. The same products she bought every month from the man who never gave his name, who accepted only cash, who'd told her once that the less she knew, the fewer problems she'd have.

"Mom." Emily was reading over her shoulder. "That's—"

"I know what it is."

The receipt paper was thin between her fingers, the kind that faded if you left it in sunlight too long. Mrs. Chen had a drawer full of identical slips at the salon—same address, same handwriting, same careful omission of any name that could be traced. She'd never thought about where they went after she filed them. Never thought about who else might have matching ones.

"How long?" Emily's voice was flat. Not angry. Worse than angry.

"Since 2019. Maybe earlier." Mrs. Chen folded the receipt along its existing crease and slipped it into her apron pocket. The motion felt automatic, the habit of a woman who'd learned not to leave evidence lying around. "He raised his prices. I asked Jay if he knew anyone else. He gave me the address."

Outside, voices had gathered—the locksmith talking to someone, explaining something about the lock mechanism, how it hadn't been forced. Mrs. Chen could hear Mrs. Patterson's granddaughter, the one who worked at [[Meridian Properties]], asking questions in that professional tone people used when they were gathering information for someone else.

Emily moved to the filing cabinet and started checking the empty drawers more carefully, running her fingers along the seams, looking for anything left behind. She found a business card wedged against the back panel—no name, just a number and the words *temporal logistics* in small gray type.

"This isn't about clef," Emily said. "Whatever Jay was doing, it wasn't just selling to tourists."

Mrs. Chen thought about the boxes she'd never opened. The products she'd never questioned. The years of not asking finally demanding an answer.

Emily pocketed the business card before Mrs. Chen could object. The motion was quick, practiced—the same efficiency her father had shown when he'd worked the register at the salon's old location, back when they'd had a register worth working. Mrs. Chen opened her mouth to say something about evidence, about leaving things where you found them, but the words died before they reached her lips. What did it matter? She'd already taken the receipt. Already made herself complicit in whatever this was.

"We should go." Emily was at the curtain, holding it aside. "Before they start asking why we're still back here."

Through the shop's front window, Mrs. Chen could see Mrs. Patterson's granddaughter—[[Angela, the one who'd gone to Stanford]]—writing something in a small notebook. The locksmith had stepped away, phone pressed to his ear. Two tourists lingered at the edge of the gathering, their too-smooth faces arranged in expressions of polite concern.

Mrs. Chen's hands found the receipt in her apron pocket. The paper was warm now, body temperature, like it had always belonged there.

"The address," she said. "International Boulevard."

Emily turned. Her expression was careful, waiting.

"I could take you." The words came out smaller than Mrs. Chen intended. "I know where it is. The man who runs it—he won't talk to strangers. But he knows me."

It was the first time she'd offered to lead Emily anywhere since the girl was small enough to need leading. The shop felt smaller with the decision made, the air thicker, as if the walls understood something had changed.
